newsitem.title: JAPAN: Mazda names Ford executive to run N.American units.
newsitem.headline: Mazda names Ford executive to run N.American units.

text.p: Japan's Mazda Motor Corp on Friday named an executive of Ford Motor Co to take the helm of the company's loss-making North American subsidiaries.

Ford's already strong grip on the Japanese carmaker will be strengthened further after Ford's Richard Beattie takes over Mazda's U.S. and Canadian operations as a specially appointed assistant to the president.

The fifth-ranked Japanese automaker also said that it was considering consolidating its five North American units, a move which the company said would help reduce costs. But it added that no job cuts are planned for now.

Mazda's long-standing ties with Ford intensified last year when Henry Wallace, a Ford official who was seconded to Mazda, took over as president at the Japanese carmaker with the task of steering the troubled firm back to prosperity.
Ford increased its stake in Mazda to one-third from 24.54 percent last April, gaining it management control.
A few months later, Wallace was appointed president, becoming the first foreigner to head a major Japanese firm.
Wallace said on Friday that the new North American chief's initial responsibility will be to create a strategic plan for integrating Mazda's five units in the area.
"Our goal is to increase market share in North America while achieving a higher level of operational efficiency," he said in a statement.

"This means we'll be focusing on improving Mazda's customer services, strengthening our U.S. and Canadian dealer networks and enhancing our overall marketing capabilities. Richard's extensive international experience was key to our naming him to head up this important position," he said.
Beattie, an executive director of Ford's Americas and Worldwide Export operations, is charged with directing efforts to strengthen Mazda's position in the North American market.
The appointment will be effective March 1.
Beattie, 42, a Briton, joined Ford in 1990. He has held posts such as executive director of Ford's Rental, Lease and Remarketing Operations and vice president of U.S. Sales and Marketing for Jaguar.
Mazda said Beattie will report directly to Wallace and will be based at Mazda Motor of America headquarters in California.
The Mazda spokesman said that the company's poor business performance in North America was behind the decision.

He said the company may consolidate its three sales units in the area but flatly denied a Japanese media report on Friday that Mazda plans to cut about 20 percent of the 1,500 workers at its units in the United States and Canada.
"We are not considering any reduction in our labour force (in the North American units) as was reported. There will be no such job cuts," he said, when asked about the report.
He also denied the same media report that Mazda would transfer some of its North American operations to Ford.

The business daily Nihon Keizai Shimbun reported that Mazda plans to cut its North American work force by 20 percent as a result of the consolidation, and also said the carmaker may transfer some operations to Ford in the future.

In November, Mazda said it expected to post a group net loss of four billion yen ($33.3 million) for 1996/97, against a May forecast of a group net profit of 10 billion yen ($83.3 million). It posted a net loss of 11.88 billion yen ($99.0 million) a year earlier, due to poor sales at home and abroad.
Mazda's sales in North America fell to 263,366 vehicles in calendar 1996 from 309,070 in 1995.
This compared with a peak of 419,213 units marked in 1994. ($1=120 yen)
